# ADR-0011: Expressions instead of plugins

> **Status:** accepted | **Date:** 2026-07-29

**References:** [RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license), [RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx), [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec), [RFC-0002:C-EXPRESSION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-expression), [RFC-0002:C-EXTENSION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-extension), [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo), [RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory), [RFC-0002:C-ORIGIN](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-origin), [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit), [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host), [RFC-0004:C-PORT-GATE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-port-gate), [RFC-0007:C-PROVENANCE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-provenance)

## Context

QGIS's moat is a plugin ecosystem of a thousand extensions, which makes "this project needs a plugin
system" look obvious. It does not survive contact with the contracts already in force.

An operator here is bound by a memory ceiling ([RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory) 1), a correct halo declaration
([RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 3), ordered reduction ([RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 3), and honest declaration of divergence
([RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx) 1). Every one of those fails silently when violated. An operator that under-declares
its halo width produces wrong answers along every partition boundary, and [RFC-0007:C-PROVENANCE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-provenance) would
faithfully record that nothing was amiss. QGIS can accept arbitrary plugin algorithms because its
processing algorithms are largely thin wrappers over GDAL and PDAL, which own the correctness; here the
operators *are* the differentiated work, so that arrangement is unavailable.

Rust having no stable ABI turned out to be a non-issue. [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 3 already requires plain Arrow
at every operator boundary, precisely so batches cross the Arrow C data interface unchanged — the data
boundary was solved as a side effect of an earlier decision.

Two needs are conflated under "plugins" and pull opposite ways: operators are compute-heavy inner loops
under hard contracts, while automation is orchestration touching none of them. Separating them was
necessary but insufficient, because the initially proposed line — orchestration may not implement an
operator — falls in the wrong place. The gap between the two is large, and the most-wanted extension sits
inside it: a custom attribute predicate is unambiguously a mapping operator, and it is what PDAL provides
as an expression filter and what QGIS provides as expressions throughout. Forbidding it makes an automation
layer useless.

Examining why that case felt safe produced the actual boundary. A pure function of one point's attributes
cannot under-declare a halo, because it has no access to other points; cannot exceed a memory ceiling or
reach an ambient capability, because it holds no state and performs no I/O; and cannot make a reduction
order-dependent, because it is pure. The contracts are not enforced against it — they are unreachable from
it. The boundary is therefore **expressiveness**, not category.

A scale constraint narrowed it further, on the reasoning [RFC-0002:C-EXPRESSION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-expression) 2's rationale sets out:
the vectorised requirement excludes arbitrary control flow and user-defined calls on performance grounds
alone. That mattered to the decision because it means purity is not a restriction this design imposes for
tidiness — it arrives twice, once from the security argument and once from the arithmetic, and an option that
kept only one of the two justifications was never available.

Finally, a serialised pipeline format turned out to already exist. [RFC-0007:C-PROVENANCE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-provenance) 2 requires the
document graph to be recorded, so the recorded graph *is* a pipeline description — the arrangement PDAL has
carried in production for a decade.

The embedded-Python option was assessed and rejected on grounds that are mostly structural rather than
about Python: CPython requires a filesystem, the global interpreter lock makes
[RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) 3's "correct single-threaded, differing only in throughput" unachievable, and it cannot
target a constrained host. The ecosystem argument for it — numpy, scipy, scikit-learn — concerns *analysis
of results* rather than the inner loop, and that is already served: a committed run writes Arrow, which
Python reads natively with no binding work.

## Decision

There is no plugin mechanism. Operators are written in-tree or by consumers building against the published
crates; pipelines are the serialised document graph; user-supplied logic is limited to declarative per-point
expressions; and operator origin is recorded and surfaced. The obligations are written in
[RFC-0002:C-EXTENSION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-extension), [RFC-0002:C-EXPRESSION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-expression) and [RFC-0002:C-ORIGIN](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-origin); this ADR records only *why*.

Why **no plugin mechanism** in the usual sense:

- **The contracts are unenforceable across a plugin boundary.** No sandbox can check that a halo declaration
  is correct, and an under-declared halo produces wrong answers at every partition boundary while provenance
  records that all was well.
- **Native dynamic loading breaks two host obligations outright.** Ambient filesystem and network access
  contradicts [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host), and dynamic loading does not exist on a constrained target, contradicting
  [RFC-0004:C-PORT-GATE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-port-gate) 1. A fault in a loaded library also terminates the process holding unsaved work.
- **Building against the crates is a genuine path, not a consolation.** [RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license) 1 publishes
  them permissively precisely so a third party can build — and sell — a tool on these operators.
- **The data ABI was never the problem.** [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 3 already requires plain Arrow at operator
  boundaries so batches cross the Arrow C data interface unchanged.

Why the boundary is **expressiveness, not category**, which corrects the first attempt at this line:

- **"Orchestration may not implement an operator" excludes the thing users most want.** A custom attribute
  predicate is a mapping operator, and it is PDAL's expression filter and QGIS's expressions throughout.
  Forbidding it makes an automation layer useless.
- **A per-point pure function cannot violate anything.** With no access to other points it cannot
  under-declare a halo; holding no state and doing no I/O it cannot exceed a ceiling or reach an ambient
  capability; being pure it cannot make a reduction order-dependent. The contracts are unreachable rather
  than checked, so admitting expressions needs no enforcement machinery.
- **Scale narrows it further.** At billions of points, per-row interpreter invocation is unusable, so an
  expression must compile to whole-array Arrow operations — ruling out arbitrary control flow and
  user-defined calls, which independently reinforces purity.
- **PDAL and QGIS arrived here separately**, which is reasonable evidence it is the right size for this
  surface.

Why the **pipeline format is the document graph**: [RFC-0007:C-PROVENANCE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-provenance) 5 already requires the graph to
be recorded, so the recorded graph is a pipeline description — PDAL's arrangement, at no cost. Requiring one
representation rather than two prevents a pipeline format and a document format drifting into disagreement
about semantics.

Why operator origin is **surfaced and not merely recorded**, the accountability decision: the argument is
[RFC-0002:C-ORIGIN](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-origin) 3's rationale, which applies [RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx) 3's reasoning to provenance. Two
alternatives it beat belong here rather than there. Admitting first-party operators only would have made the
permissive licensing pointless, since the point of the licence is that others build on this. Admitting anything
with an open caveat-emptor notice would have hollowed out a provenance guarantee already paid for elsewhere in
the corpus. And verification may not be self-asserted, or the marker means nothing — which is what rules out
the cheap middle option of letting an author declare their own operator verified.

A sandboxed WebAssembly mechanism remains the intended eventual answer for third-party operators, deferred
rather than declined: its capability model closely matches the injection [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) already
requires, and [RFC-0004:C-PORT-GATE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-port-gate) 1 means the host side is being built regardless.

## Consequences

### Positive

The common extension need is met with no enforcement machinery, because expressions cannot reach the
contracts they might otherwise break. Pipelines are serialisable for free, since provenance already demands
it. No sandbox, no interpreter, no dynamic loading, and no plugin fault can terminate a session. Third
parties can still build commercially on the operators, which is what permissive licensing was for. And
operator origin costs nothing to record, riding on the evaluation configuration already kept per committed
run.

### Negative

There is no drop-in ecosystem, so a third-party operator requires compiling against the crates — a real
barrier compared with QGIS. Expressions cannot describe neighbourhood logic, so genuine needs beyond
attribute predicates go unserved until a sandboxed mechanism exists. Verification status requires a reviewer
who is not the author, which is a process the project has to actually run rather than a field it can add.

### Neutral

Adaptive orchestration — retry with wider parameters, branch on intermediate results — is unavailable,
deferred to a command-line interface and shell loops on the grounds that forestry batch work is parallel
over files. Whether that reads as a gap depends on whether such workflows appear.

Three drifts to watch. First, an automation facility acquiring the ability to introduce an operator, which
would be an escape hatch around every contract in the specification and is why [RFC-0002:C-EXTENSION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-extension) 3
forbids it before any such facility exists. Second, expressions growing control flow or user-defined
functions in response to a reasonable-sounding request, which would forfeit both vectorised evaluation and
the purity that makes them safe. Third, verification status becoming author-asserted because finding
reviewers is slow — the field then means nothing while continuing to look like it means something, which is
worse than not having it.

Reversal cost is low in one direction only. Adding a sandboxed operator mechanism later is additive and its
conditions are already stated in [RFC-0002:C-EXTENSION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-extension) 4. Withdrawing an extension surface once third
parties depend on it is not available, which is the reason for starting narrow.

## Alternatives Considered

### No plugin mechanism: operators are written in-tree or by consumers building against the published crates; pipelines are the serialised document graph; user logic is limited to declarative per-point expressions; operator origin is recorded and unverified output is surfaced like approximate output (accepted)

- **Pros:** Expressions are safe by construction — every contract they could violate is unreachable from them, Covers the overwhelmingly common extension need with no enforcement machinery, The pipeline format already exists, since the document graph must be serialised for provenance, Permissive licensing means building against the crates is a real path, not a restriction, Operator origin rides on the evaluation configuration already recorded per committed run
- **Cons:** No third-party operators without compiling, so no drop-in ecosystem, Expressions cannot express neighbourhood logic, so some genuine needs go unserved, Verification status requires a reviewer who is not the author, which is process the project must run

### Sandboxed operators compiled to WebAssembly, with capabilities supplied explicitly

- **Pros:** A capability-supplying sandbox is a close match to the injection model [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) already requires, Portable, language-agnostic, and cannot reach ambient filesystem or network, A fault is contained rather than terminating the process holding unsaved work, The host side is being built anyway, since [RFC-0004:C-PORT-GATE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-port-gate) 1 requires the core to target a constrained host
- **Cons:** Contract conformance is still unenforceable: a sandbox cannot check a halo declaration is correct, Overhead on compute-heavy inner loops, and Arrow buffers must cross a linear-memory boundary carefully, Substantial machinery before the out-of-core claim is demonstrated

### Natively compiled dynamic libraries loaded at runtime, as CloudCompare and GDAL do (rejected)

- **Pros:** Native speed with no boundary overhead; the established model in this field, Third parties ship binaries users drop in, giving a real ecosystem, Arrow's C data interface provides a stable data ABI despite Rust having none
- **Cons:** Ambient filesystem and network access, so [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) cannot hold, No dynamic loading on a constrained target, breaking [RFC-0004:C-PORT-GATE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-port-gate) 1, A fault in a plugin terminates the process holding the user's unsaved work
- **Rejected because:** It cannot satisfy the host-capability obligations, since a loaded native library has ambient access by construction, and it cannot exist on a target without dynamic loading. It also makes a third party's defect indistinguishable from ours at the point of a crash. Building against permissively licensed crates achieves the same extensibility without any of it.

### Embedded Python interpreter for operators and automation, as QGIS does (rejected)

- **Pros:** Immediate access to numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and the scientific Python ecosystem, The lowest barrier to contribution of any option, and familiar to the target users, Proven at scale by QGIS's plugin ecosystem
- **Cons:** CPython requires a filesystem, breaching [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) 1, The interpreter lock makes [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) 3's single-threaded-correctness-differing-only-in-throughput unachievable, Cannot target a constrained host, breaking [RFC-0004:C-PORT-GATE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-port-gate) 1, Per-point interpreter invocation is unusable at billions of points
- **Rejected because:** It breaches three host obligations at once and cannot be made to satisfy them. The ecosystem argument concerns analysis of results rather than inner loops, and that need is already met: a committed run writes Arrow, which Python reads natively with no binding work. Embedding an interpreter would buy little that Arrow output does not already provide, at the cost of the portability regime.

### Embedded scripting language for orchestration in the first release: adaptive parameter search, conditional flow, batch loops (rejected)

- **Pros:** Enables workflows expressions cannot: retry with wider parameters, branch on intermediate results, Familiar to users of every comparable tool
- **Cons:** Reintroduces the sandboxing problem the no-plugin decision avoided, through a side door, Interpreter, sandbox and API surface to build and maintain, in the least differentiated part of the product, Batch work over files is embarrassingly parallel, so a shell loop over a command-line interface already does it
- **Rejected because:** The orchestration it enables is achievable without it — forestry batch work is parallel over files, so a shell loop over a command-line interface suffices — while the machinery it requires is exactly the sandboxing problem declining a plugin mechanism was meant to avoid. Deferred rather than dismissed: if adaptive workflows prove necessary, this is the shape they take.
